stem: A developer maintaining a Bedrock-integrated Lambda function is unsure why a boto3 call is failing with a specific validation exception and wants an in-IDE explanation along with a suggested code fix, without leaving their editor or manually searching documentation. What should they use?

choices.text: AWS Config rules for Lambda
Amazon QuickSight Q
Amazon Q Developer in the IDE
AWS Trusted Advisor checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Q Developer in the IDE can explain an error in context, suggest a fix, and answer AWS SDK questions without leaving the editor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config rules: compliance of resources.
• QuickSight Q: natural-language BI questions.
• Trusted Advisor: account best-practice checks.

Key takeaway: in-IDE code help → Q Developer.

stem: A team is deciding whether to implement a multi-step RAG-plus-classification workflow using Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows' visual builder or a custom AWS Step Functions state machine with Lambda tasks. Prompt Flows offers faster iteration for prompt engineers but is more limited for complex custom logic, while Step Functions offers full programmatic flexibility at the cost of more development effort. Which factor would most justify choosing Step Functions over Prompt Flows for this workflow?

choices.text: When cost is not a meaningful factor, because Prompt Flows is priced higher than Step Functions at any volume
When the workflow is a simple two-step prompt chain with no external integrations
When non-developers need the fastest iteration without writing code
When it needs complex custom logic and integrations (Textract, DynamoDB conditional writes, human callbacks)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions is better when the workflow needs arbitrary AWS integrations (Textract, DynamoDB conditional writes), complex branching, and human-in-the-loop callbacks. Prompt Flows is optimized for visual prompt chaining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost framing: not the deciding factor stated.
• Simple two-step chains: fit Prompt Flows well.
• Non-developers iterating quickly: again a Prompt Flows strength.

Key takeaway: complex logic and integrations → Step Functions; visual prompt chains → Prompt Flows.

stem: A customer-facing Bedrock chatbot must block hate, violence, sexual, and insult content in both user inputs and model outputs. Product wants stricter blocking on inputs than on outputs, and the team must not write custom classifiers. Which configuration meets these requirements?

choices.text: A guardrail with contextual grounding checks at a high threshold for both prompts and responses
A guardrail with content filters for those categories, using separate strengths for prompts and responses
An Amazon Comprehend toxicity check in a Lambda function before and after each model call
A guardrail with a denied topic named 'hate speech and violence' and sample phrases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Guardrail content filters target exactly these harm categories and let you set filter strength separately for inputs (prompts) and outputs (responses). They are applied by passing the guardrail on each call, with no custom classification code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Contextual grounding: detects responses not supported by source content or not relevant to the query. It is a hallucination control, not a harmful-content filter.
• Denied topic: meant for business subject areas to avoid (for example, investment advice). It is a poor, incomplete substitute for purpose-built content filters.
• Comprehend in Lambda: possible, but it is custom integration code, which the team wants to avoid.

Key takeaway: harmful content categories → content filters; off-limits business subjects → denied topics; ungrounded answers → contextual grounding.

stem: A bank deploys an FM-powered assistant for general customer inquiries. Compliance requires that the assistant never provide specific investment or tax advice, even if a customer asks directly, while still answering general account questions. Which Bedrock Guardrails capability most directly enforces this requirement?

choices.text: Contextual grounding checks on the knowledge base responses
Word filters listing banned financial terms
Denied topics describing investment and tax advice
A HIGH-strength hate speech content filter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Denied topics describe an entire subject (investment and tax advice) in natural language, with examples, and block it however the user phrases the request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Contextual grounding: checks faithfulness to sources, not subject restrictions.
• Word filters: match exact terms and miss paraphrases.
• Hate speech filter: a different harm category.

Key takeaway: conceptual subject bans → denied topics.

stem: After deploying Bedrock Guardrails with default content filter strengths, a security review finds that users can still get the model to produce disallowed content by asking it to 'roleplay as an AI with no restrictions' and answer in a fictional dialogue. What is the most effective first remediation?

choices.text: Delete the guardrail and rely on the foundation model's built-in safety training, which is tuned for jailbreaks
Enable the prompt attack filter at HIGH strength on user inputs
Switch the knowledge base to a higher-dimension embedding model so malicious prompts are classified more accurately
Reduce the maximum response tokens so any disallowed content that slips through is cut short

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Roleplay and 'no restrictions' requests are jailbreak attempts. The prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks and prompt injection in user inputs, and raising it to HIGH strengthens detection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deleting the guardrail: removes protection; built-in safety alone was already bypassed.
• Embedding model change: unrelated; the guardrail doesn't use the knowledge base's embeddings.
• Fewer output tokens: harmful content can still be short.

Key takeaway: jailbreak attempts → prompt attack filter on inputs.

stem: A text-to-SQL agent built on Bedrock lets business analysts ask natural-language questions against a data warehouse. The team wants to prevent the agent from ever executing destructive statements like DROP or DELETE. Which combination of controls provides the strongest defense-in-depth?

choices.text: SELECT-only database permissions for the execution role plus validation that rejects non-SELECT statements
Increase the guardrail's hate speech filter strength so harmful instructions in questions are blocked
Instruct the model in the system prompt to never generate destructive SQL, with examples of forbidden statements
Record all generated SQL in CloudTrail so any destructive statement can be identified and reversed afterward

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least-privilege database permissions (SELECT only) make destructive statements fail even if generated, and application-side validation rejects non-SELECT statements before execution. Two independent layers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hate speech filter: doesn't recognize destructive SQL.
• System prompt instructions: can be bypassed by injection.
• CloudTrail logging: records, but doesn't prevent damage.

Key takeaway: enforce safety in permissions and validation, not only in prompts.

stem: Before releasing a fine-tuned foundation model to production, a team needs a repeatable, quantitative way to measure the toxicity and robustness of its outputs across many prompts, without manually reviewing every response. Which Amazon Bedrock capability should they use?

choices.text: Bedrock Knowledge Bases hybrid search results
Bedrock Provisioned Throughput benchmarks
Bedrock Agents multi-agent collaboration tests
Bedrock model evaluation jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock model evaluation jobs run automatic evaluations over a prompt dataset with built-in metrics such as toxicity and robustness, giving repeatable, quantitative results before release.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Knowledge Base hybrid search: retrieval.
• Provisioned Throughput benchmarks: capacity, not output safety.
• Multi-agent collaboration tests: orchestration.

Key takeaway: repeatable quality and safety scoring → model evaluation jobs.

stem: A text-to-SQL assistant occasionally generates a query with a Cartesian join that returns billions of rows, causing warehouse timeouts and cost spikes. Guardrails content filters do not flag this because the text itself is not harmful. What should the team add to prevent this specific failure mode?

choices.text: A pre-execution SQL validator that checks join conditions and enforces row or cost limits
A stricter Bedrock guardrail misconduct filter applied to the generated query text
Amazon Macie scanning of each generated query before it reaches the warehouse
A larger context window so the model sees the full schema and join keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A validator inspects generated SQL before running it (for example, requiring join conditions and using EXPLAIN or cost estimates) and enforces row or cost limits, stopping runaway queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Misconduct filter: targets harmful language, not SQL correctness.
• Macie: sensitive data in S3, not query analysis.
• Larger context window: may help but doesn't guarantee safe queries.

Key takeaway: generated code needs execution-time validation.

stem: Users of a Bedrock Knowledge Bases-powered support assistant report they cannot tell whether an answer came from an official policy document or was inferred. Which combination of features best improves trust and verifiability of answers?

choices.text: Add a denied topics list for policy questions
Enable source citations and a contextual grounding threshold
Disable the vector store so answers come consistently from the model's own knowledge
Increase the temperature so answers paraphrase policies less literally

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Citations from RetrieveAndGenerate link each answer to its source chunks, and a contextual grounding threshold filters claims not supported by the retrieved content, so users can tell sourced facts from inference.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Denied topics: would block policy questions.
• Disabling the vector store: removes the sources entirely.
• Higher temperature: more variation and less faithfulness.

Key takeaway: traceable answers = citations + grounding checks.

stem: A team is deciding how to detect potential hallucinations in a Bedrock RAG pipeline. Option one is Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check; option two is capturing the model's own self-reported confidence score in the prompt response. What is the key limitation of relying solely on option two?

choices.text: Confidence scores require a separate VPC endpoint and cannot be enabled in the same workload
Self-reported scores come from the same model and are not verified against sources
Confidence scores are supported only for text-to-SQL and classification use cases
Confidence scores cannot be logged to CloudWatch, so hallucination rates cannot be tracked

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A model's self-reported confidence comes from the same generation that produced the answer, so it can be confidently wrong. A grounding check compares the answer with the retrieved evidence independently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC endpoint requirement: not a real restriction.
• Only for text-to-SQL: not a real restriction.
• Can't log to CloudWatch: scores can be logged; the problem is reliability.

Key takeaway: verify against evidence; don't trust self-assessment alone.

stem: A generative AI application uses Amazon API Gateway as the entry point, AWS Lambda for request orchestration, Amazon Comprehend for text analysis, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for model-level safety. The architecture team wants to identify which two layers are best suited to reject malformed or oversized requests and detect PII in free-text fields BEFORE the request ever reaches the foundation model. (Select TWO.)

choices.text: SageMaker Model Monitor data quality checks
API Gateway request validation and payload limits
Bedrock model evaluation jobs on each request
Comprehend PII detection from the Lambda orchestrator
Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding check on inputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway request validation and payload limits reject malformed or oversized requests before any compute runs, and Comprehend PII detection called from Lambda inspects free text before it reaches the model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model Monitor data quality: monitors SageMaker endpoints, not request validation here.
• Evaluation jobs per request: offline evaluation, not a runtime input check.
• Grounding check on inputs: grounding evaluates responses against sources.

Key takeaway: validate inputs at the edge and scan text before the model sees it.

stem: A security audit finds that an application's only safety control is a single Bedrock Guardrail attached to the InvokeModel call, and a red-team exercise bypassed it using a base64-encoded instruction embedded in an uploaded document that is later summarized by the model. What architectural change best addresses this gap?

choices.text: Add a pre-processing step that decodes, normalizes, and scans document content before it enters the prompt
Replace the guardrail with a much longer denied topics list covering every encoding trick found by the red team
Increase only the guardrail's response filter strength so any harmful output generated from documents is blocked
Move the application from Lambda to Amazon EC2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The bypass came through document content (indirect injection with encoding tricks). Decoding, normalizing, and scanning content before it enters the prompt adds a second, independent layer ahead of the guardrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer denied topics list: can't enumerate every encoding trick.
• Response filter only: the injected instructions still steer the model.
• Moving to EC2: compute platform doesn't matter.

Key takeaway: defense in depth: sanitize untrusted content before prompting.

stem: A RAG-based assistant retrieves and summarizes third-party web pages stored in a knowledge base. An attacker publishes a page containing hidden text instructing the model to ignore its system prompt and reveal internal configuration. Which set of controls most directly mitigates this indirect prompt injection risk?

choices.text: Disable citations in RetrieveAndGenerate so the model cannot reference the attacker's page directly
Rely on the embedding model to down-rank malicious text, since injected instructions have unusual embeddings
Apply prompt attack detection to the assembled prompt and treat retrieved content as untrusted data
Increase the knowledge base chunk size so hidden text is diluted by the surrounding legitimate content

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieved web content is untrusted. Scanning the assembled prompt for prompt-attack patterns and clearly delimiting retrieved text as data (not instructions) mitigates indirect injection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling citations: hides the source; the injection still works.
• Relying on embeddings: embeddings don't detect malicious instructions.
• Bigger chunks: dilution doesn't neutralize instructions.

Key takeaway: treat retrieved content as data, never as commands.

stem: Logs show that a jailbreak succeeded only after a long multi-turn conversation where each individual message passed guardrail checks, but the cumulative context gradually led the model to violate policy. What is the most effective mitigation?

choices.text: Disable multi-turn conversations entirely and require users to restate full context in every single message
Check only the first message of each session more strictly
Evaluate the full conversation context and cap session length to trigger re-evaluation or reset
Increase the model's maximum output tokens so its refusals are complete and not cut off mid-turn

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gradual multi-turn jailbreaks slip past checks on single messages. Evaluating guardrails against the accumulated conversation and capping session length (with reset or re-evaluation) catches the drift.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling multi-turn: breaks the product.
• Checking only the first message: misses later drift entirely.
• More output tokens: unrelated.

Key takeaway: evaluate conversations, not just messages.

stem: A company wants only its 'ml-research' IAM role to be able to invoke a specific set of approved, cost-controlled foundation models in Bedrock, while blocking that role from invoking any other model. Which approach best achieves this?

choices.text: An IAM policy on the ml-research role allowing bedrock:InvokeModel only on approved model ARNs
A CloudWatch alarm on invocation counts per model that notifies when other roles call them
A Bedrock guardrail with denied topics for unapproved models
An S3 bucket policy on the model artifacts bucket restricting reads to the role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An IAM policy that allows bedrock:InvokeModel (and InvokeModelWithResponseStream) only on the approved model ARNs lets the role use those models, and everything else is implicitly denied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch alarm: detects after the fact; doesn't block.
• Guardrail denied topics: control content, not which model can be called.
• S3 bucket policy: Bedrock foundation models aren't accessed through your bucket.

Key takeaway: which models a principal can call → IAM resource scoping.

stem: Multiple ML teams share a single S3-based feature store used to fine-tune foundation models. Team A should see only anonymized columns, while Team B (with special approval) can see raw PII columns in the same tables. What is the primary advantage of using AWS Lake Formation over IAM-only S3 bucket policies here?

choices.text: Lake Formation is required to enable encryption at rest for tables shared between teams
Lake Formation adds column- and row-level access control on the same tables without copying data
Lake Formation replaces the need for encryption or KMS keys by controlling access at the catalog level
IAM policies cannot be used with S3 data that is registered in the Glue Data Catalog

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation adds column- and row-level permissions on Glue Data Catalog tables, so Team A and Team B query the same data with different visible columns, without copies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Required for encryption: encryption is separate (S3/KMS).
• Replaces encryption: it doesn't.
• IAM can't be used with cataloged data: IAM still applies.

Key takeaway: fine-grained access on shared tables → Lake Formation.

stem: A SageMaker notebook instance launched inside a private VPC subnet with no internet gateway or NAT gateway fails when calling the Bedrock InvokeModel API, returning a connection timeout. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The private subnet has no route to Bedrock; add an interface VPC endpoint for Bedrock
The notebook instance type is too small to establish TLS connections to Bedrock's regional endpoint
The notebook's IAM execution role is missing the bedrock:InvokeModel permission for the requested model
A Bedrock guardrail attached to the account is blocking all requests coming from SageMaker

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A private subnet with no NAT gateway or endpoint has no route to Bedrock's endpoint, so connections time out. An interface VPC endpoint for Bedrock Runtime provides a private path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Instance too small: doesn't prevent TLS connections.
• Missing IAM permission: would return AccessDenied, not a timeout.
• Guardrail blocking: guardrails don't block network connections.

Key takeaway: timeouts from private subnets usually mean no network path; add endpoints.

stem: An organization needs to share curated training datasets across three AWS accounts belonging to different business units, with centrally managed, auditable, fine-grained permissions that can be granted or revoked without rewriting bucket policies in every account. Which approach is best suited?

choices.text: Make the bucket public with a resource policy that restricts access by referrer header per business unit
Copy the source bucket policy into each consuming account and grant each account's roles access
Lake Formation cross-account sharing with permissions defined centrally in the Data Catalog
Share IAM access keys for a dedicated data-reader user with each business unit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lake Formation cross-account sharing grants fine-grained, centrally managed, audited permissions on catalog tables to other accounts without duplicating bucket policies or data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public bucket with referrer checks: insecure and easily spoofed.
• Copied bucket policies: don't scale and lack fine-grained control.
• Shared IAM keys: long-term credentials without accountability.

Key takeaway: cross-account governed data sharing → Lake Formation.

stem: Before fine-tuning a foundation model on a large S3 data lake of scanned customer documents, a data science team wants to identify which objects contain sensitive information like credit card numbers or national ID numbers so those objects can be excluded or remediated. Which service is purpose-built for this discovery task at the S3 object level?

choices.text: AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon Macie
Amazon Comprehend Custom Classification
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie scans S3 objects at scale with managed and custom data identifiers to find sensitive data such as PII before it's used for fine-tuning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue crawlers: infer schemas, not sensitive content.
• Comprehend Custom Classification: classifies documents; not built for estate-wide S3 discovery.
• Guardrails: runtime controls for model inputs and outputs.

Key takeaway: find sensitive data in S3 → Macie.

stem: A company has two privacy needs. Need 1: redact customer names and phone numbers from each chat message in real time before it is sent to a model. Need 2: find out which of its 3,000 S3 buckets contain PII and keep that inventory current. Which assignment of services is correct?

choices.text: Comprehend (or guardrails) for need 1; Macie for need 2
Amazon Macie for both needs, since it detects PII in text and in S3
Amazon Comprehend for both needs, running batch PII jobs over every bucket for need 2
Amazon Macie for need 1 and Amazon Comprehend for need 2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comprehend's PII detection works on individual text in near real time, which fits redacting each message inline. Guardrail sensitive information filters are another option in a Bedrock flow. Macie discovers sensitive data at rest across S3, with automated discovery and an inventory across many buckets, which fits need 2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Macie for both: Macie analyzes S3 objects and is not an inline API for redacting messages in a request path.
• Comprehend for both: you could build batch jobs, but you'd reinvent bucket inventory, sampling, and continuous discovery that Macie provides.
• Swapped assignment: each service would be used for the job it is not designed for.

Key takeaway: inline text redaction → Comprehend or guardrails; estate-wide S3 sensitive data discovery → Macie.

stem: Amazon Macie reports that a fine-tuning dataset in S3 contains unmasked social security numbers in free-text fields. The dataset must still be used for fine-tuning after remediation. What is the most appropriate remediation workflow?

choices.text: Block public access on the bucket and proceed with fine-tuning, since private data is not exposed externally
Encrypt the bucket with a customer managed KMS key and treat encryption as resolving the finding
Mask the values with Comprehend PII redaction (or DataBrew), then re-run Macie to confirm no findings remain
Accept the findings, because data used only for fine-tuning is out of scope for the privacy requirements

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The data must be usable but without SSNs, so the values must actually be masked or redacted (for example, with Comprehend PII redaction or DataBrew), then Macie is re-run to confirm the findings are gone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking public access: SSNs remain in the dataset.
• KMS encryption: protects storage, but the model still trains on SSNs.
• Accepting findings: violates privacy requirements.

Key takeaway: remediate PII by removing it, then verify.

stem: A team is choosing between (1) using Bedrock Guardrails PII masking at inference time only, versus (2) scrubbing PII from the training corpus with Comprehend before fine-tuning. What is the key risk of relying on option (1) alone?

choices.text: A model trained on PII may memorize it and leak it indirectly in ways a runtime filter misses
Guardrails can mask only a small fixed set of PII types that excludes most personal identifiers
Comprehend can run only inside Amazon Bedrock
Guardrails PII masking costs more per request than Comprehend, making runtime masking uneconomical

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A model fine-tuned on PII can memorize it and reproduce it in unexpected forms that runtime pattern filters miss. Scrubbing training data prevents memorization in the first place.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guardrails supports only a few types: it supports many configurable PII types.
• Comprehend only inside Bedrock: Comprehend is a standalone service.
• Cost comparison: not the key risk.

Key takeaway: clean training data; runtime filters can't undo memorization.

stem: A dataset had direct identifiers (names, SSNs) removed before being used for FM fine-tuning, but a privacy audit later shows individuals can still be re-identified by combining quasi-identifiers like ZIP code, birth date, and gender that remained in the data. What does this indicate about the anonymization approach used?

choices.text: Re-identification risk applies only to structured tables, not to free-text data used for fine-tuning
Removing direct identifiers is not enough; quasi-identifiers need generalization or k-anonymity
The data was fully anonymized once direct identifiers were removed
Encrypting the dataset at rest with KMS would have prevented individuals from being re-identified

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Combinations of quasi-identifiers (such as ZIP code, birth date, and gender) can still single out people. Techniques such as generalization, suppression, or k-anonymity are needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Structured-only risk: free text can also contain quasi-identifiers.
• Fully anonymized after removing identifiers: the audit shows it wasn't.
• Encryption: doesn't affect what authorized users can infer.

Key takeaway: anonymization must address quasi-identifiers too.

stem: A healthcare support assistant must retain the ability for support agents to reference a patient's phone number for callback purposes, but must never expose the patient's full Social Security number in any generated response. When configuring PII handling in Bedrock Guardrails, what is the appropriate configuration?

choices.text: Set SSN to Block and phone number to Mask (or allow)
Set both SSN and phone number to Block so neither ever appears
Disable PII filtering and rely on agents to redact manually
Set both to Mask with the same character

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Guardrails lets you set actions per PII entity type: Block for SSNs (never shown) and Mask or allow for phone numbers that agents need.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Block both: removes a needed capability.
• Manual redaction: unreliable.
• Mask both the same way: SSN exposure risk remains if masking fails, and it doesn't match the need.

Key takeaway: configure PII handling per entity type.

stem: A hospital's generative AI application needs to mask internal patient identifiers (a custom 8-digit format unique to the hospital's systems) in generated summaries, but Bedrock Guardrails' built-in PII entity types do not include this custom identifier format. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Wait for AWS to add the hospital's identifier format as a built-in Guardrails entity type
Use the built-in SSN entity type, which matches most numeric identifier formats
Train a Comprehend custom entity recognizer for the format and use it alongside Guardrails
Have staff manually review every generated summary before it is released

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For organization-specific identifier formats, a Comprehend custom entity recognizer (or guardrail regex patterns) detects them, alongside built-in PII handling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Waiting for AWS: may never happen.
• SSN entity type: won't match an 8-digit custom format reliably.
• Manual review: doesn't scale.

Key takeaway: custom sensitive formats → custom recognizers or regex filters.

stem: Auditors require, for each fine-tuned model version: intended use, risk rating, training data description, and evaluation results, tied to the exact version approved for production and exportable for review. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Rely on CloudTrail logs of the training and deployment API calls as the audit record
Document the details in AWS Glue Data Catalog table properties for the training dataset
Store the information as tags on the Model Registry model package version
Create a SageMaker Model Card per version, linked to the Model Registry version, and export it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Model Cards are structured documentation for a model: intended uses, risk rating, training details, and evaluation results. They can be versioned, linked to a model package in the Model Registry, and exported (for example, as PDF), which matches the audit requirement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Registry tags: short key-value metadata, not structured governance documentation with evaluation results.
• Glue Data Catalog properties: describe datasets, not a model's intended use or risk.
• CloudTrail: records who called which API and when. That's useful evidence, but not documentation of intended use or risk.

Key takeaway: governance documentation → Model Cards; version and approval tracking → Model Registry. Use them together.

stem: A financial services company fine-tunes a foundation model using data that passes through several AWS Glue ETL jobs before landing in the training bucket. Auditors need to trace exactly which raw source tables and transformations contributed to the final training dataset. Which capability supports this?

choices.text: AWS Glue data lineage across jobs and the Data Catalog
CloudWatch Logs Insights over the Glue job logs
Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding
SageMaker Model Cards training data section

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue data lineage tracks how data moves and transforms across Glue jobs and catalog tables, letting auditors trace training data back to its sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: operational logs, not lineage.
• Grounding checks: model output faithfulness.
• Model Card training section: describes data but doesn't trace transformations.

Key takeaway: trace data transformations → lineage.

stem: A team already uses the SageMaker Model Registry to version models and gate deployment approvals. A governance stakeholder asks why they also need SageMaker Model Cards. What is the best justification?

choices.text: The Registry tracks versions and approvals; Model Cards document intended use, risks, and evaluations
The Model Registry cannot register foundation models, so Model Cards are the only governance option
Model Cards replace the Model Registry because they also store approval status and model versions
Model Cards and the Model Registry are the same feature exposed under different names in the console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Model Registry manages versions and approval workflows. Model Cards document intended use, risks, and evaluations for governance. They're complementary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Registry can't hold FMs: not the point, and not accurate.
• Cards replace the Registry: they don't track deployment approvals.
• Same feature: they're different.

Key takeaway: Registry = lifecycle; Model Cards = documentation.

stem: A company ingests documents from multiple business units into a Bedrock Knowledge Base and needs to track and later query which sensitivity classification (public, internal, confidential) each source document had, for governance reporting. What is an effective approach?

choices.text: Tag source objects and their Data Catalog metadata with sensitivity attributes used in reports
Use CloudFront cache headers on document URLs to mark each document's sensitivity level
Let the foundation model infer sensitivity from each document's content at query time
Record the sensitivity level of each business unit's documents in the chatbot's system prompt

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tagging source objects and their catalog metadata with sensitivity classifications creates a structured, queryable record for governance reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront cache headers: control caching, not classification.
• Model inference at query time: unreliable and not auditable.
• System prompt notes: not queryable metadata.

Key takeaway: governance needs structured metadata, not model guesses.

stem: An auditor asks which IAM principal invoked a specific Bedrock agent (InvokeAgent) on a given date, but a query of CloudTrail management events shows no matching entries. What is the most likely explanation and fix?

choices.text: CloudTrail does not record Amazon Bedrock API calls, so model invocation logging must be used instead
InvokeAgent is a CloudTrail data event; data event logging for Bedrock agents must be enabled
CloudTrail retains management events for only 24 hours, so the record for that date has expired
The invocation used an IAM role, and CloudTrail records the caller only for IAM users

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock agent invocations (InvokeAgent) are CloudTrail data events, which aren't logged by default and must be enabled on a trail or event data store. (Runtime InvokeModel and Converse calls are logged as management events.)

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail doesn't record Bedrock: it does.
• 24-hour retention: event history keeps 90 days of management events.
• IAM users only: CloudTrail records role sessions too.

Key takeaway: know which calls are data events; enable them before you need them.

stem: A compliance requirement states that every answer produced by a Bedrock Knowledge Base-powered assistant must be traceable back to the specific source document, version, and ingestion date. Which combination of practices best satisfies this at the data layer?

choices.text: Instruct the model to state its sources in each answer and store the responses for audit
Tag documents with source, version, and date metadata and enable Knowledge Bases citations
Store all documents in one S3 prefix and use descriptive file names as the tracking mechanism
Enable CloudTrail data events so every retrieval call is recorded with its request parameters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Capturing source, version, and date as metadata at ingestion, plus citations at query time, ties each statement to a specific versioned source chunk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model-stated sources: unreliable.
• File names in one prefix: fragile and not linked to answers.
• CloudTrail data events: record API calls, not which chunk supported a statement.

Key takeaway: traceability is designed in at ingestion and query time.

stem: A large enterprise with dozens of AWS accounts under AWS Organizations wants to centrally prevent any account from invoking foundation models that have not been through a legal/compliance review, regardless of individual account IAM policies. What is the most effective control?

choices.text: A CloudWatch alarm that notifies security when an unapproved model is invoked
An SCP on the OU that denies InvokeModel for model ARNs not on the approved list
A Bedrock guardrail applied in the production account for unapproved models
An IAM policy deployed separately to every role in each of the accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An SCP on the OU denies bedrock:InvokeModel for any model not on the approved list, and it applies to every account in the OU regardless of their IAM policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch alarm: detective only.
• Guardrail in one account: content control, and only in that account.
• IAM policies per role: hard to keep consistent across dozens of accounts.

Key takeaway: org-wide preventive limits → SCPs.

stem: An enterprise is deciding between (1) a centralized shared-services account through which all teams access Bedrock via cross-account roles, versus (2) letting each of 20 teams manage its own direct Bedrock access in their own accounts. From a governance perspective, what is the main tradeoff?

choices.text: There is no meaningful governance difference, because IAM policies work the same way in both approaches
Per-team accounts always provide stronger security because account boundaries isolate every team fully
Centralized access eases policy, audit, and cost visibility but can bottleneck; per-team access risks inconsistency
Centralized access removes the need for IAM, since the shared-services account authenticates all callers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A central shared-services account makes guardrails, auditing, and cost allocation consistent but can slow onboarding and add role complexity. Per-team access gives autonomy at the cost of consistency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No difference: governance changes significantly.
• Per-team always stronger: isolation doesn't ensure consistent controls.
• Central removes IAM: IAM is still required.

Key takeaway: centralization trades autonomy for consistency.

stem: A governance team wants continuous, automated verification that every Bedrock Agent deployed across the organization has a Guardrail attached, flagging any agent that does not. What AWS service is best suited to continuously evaluate this configuration compliance?

choices.text: Amazon Comprehend custom classification of agent configs
Amazon Macie automated discovery on agent settings
An AWS Config rule checking for an attached guardrail
AWS Glue crawlers cataloging agent configurations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Config evaluates resource configurations continuously. A (custom) rule can flag any Bedrock agent without an associated guardrail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend classification: text analysis.
• Macie: sensitive data in S3.
• Glue crawlers: data schemas.

Key takeaway: continuous configuration compliance → Config rules.

stem: A team has fine-tuned a foundation model used for loan-eligibility summarization and wants ongoing production monitoring for both (a) whether the statistical distribution of incoming requests is drifting from the training data, and (b) whether the model's fairness/bias characteristics are drifting over time for protected groups. Which two SageMaker Model Monitor capabilities should they enable? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Prompt attack detection
Denied topics monitoring
Contextual grounding check
Data quality monitoring
Bias drift monitoring

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data quality monitoring detects drift in incoming data compared with a baseline, and bias drift monitoring (Clarify with Model Monitor) tracks changes in bias metrics over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt attack detection, denied topics, grounding: guardrail runtime controls, not drift monitoring.

Key takeaway: distribution drift → data quality monitor; fairness drift → bias drift monitor.

stem: Security notices an unusual spike in requests that are being blocked by Bedrock Guardrails' prompt-attack filter from a small set of source IP addresses/API keys over a short window, suggesting automated jailbreak probing. What is the most appropriate real-time response mechanism to configure going forward?

choices.text: Disable the prompt attack filter temporarily to reduce log noise while the traffic is investigated
Increase the model's context window so legitimate requests are not blocked alongside the attacks
Publish guardrail intervention metrics and alarm when blocked rates per identity exceed a threshold
Review CloudTrail logs quarterly to identify identities with repeated blocked requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Publishing guardrail intervention metrics per identity and alarming on spikes gives near-real-time detection, enabling alerting or automatic throttling while the abuse is happening.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling the filter: removes protection.
• Larger context window: unrelated.
• Quarterly review: far too slow.

Key takeaway: misuse detection needs real-time signals.

stem: A team is weighing real-time CloudWatch alarms on Guardrails intervention rates against a weekly batch review of aggregated invocation logs for governance monitoring. What is the main advantage of the real-time approach that the periodic approach lacks?

choices.text: Weekly batch review is more accurate because it analyzes complete aggregated data instead of partial windows
Real-time alarms detect active abuse quickly, while weekly review surfaces it after harm may occur
Periodic review cannot be automated, so it depends on analysts remembering to run it each week
Real-time alarms remove the need to retain invocation logs, which lowers storage cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Real-time alarms shorten time to detection so active abuse can be stopped quickly. A weekly review finds it after harm may have occurred.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch is more accurate: accuracy isn't the difference.
• Periodic review can't be automated: it can.
• No need to retain logs: logs remain needed for investigation and audit.

Key takeaway: monitoring cadence determines how fast you can respond.

stem: A product team is deciding whether to expose the full Bedrock Agent reasoning trace directly to end customers in a customer-facing app, versus keeping it available only to internal support staff via a separate audit view. What is the main risk of exposing the raw trace to end customers?

choices.text: Exposing traces lets customers correct the agent's reasoning, which improves accuracy over time
Traces are encrypted in transit and at rest
Traces cannot be generated for customer-facing applications because tracing is only for testing
Traces can reveal tool names, prompts, and data sources that help attackers craft injections

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Raw agent traces can reveal tool names, prompts, and data sources, which helps attackers craft targeted injections. A curated view is safer for customers, with full traces kept internal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Customers correcting reasoning: not how agents improve.
• Encryption: doesn't stop the customer from reading what's shown.
• Traces are test-only: they're available in production too.

Key takeaway: don't expose internal agent internals to end users.

stem: An FM-powered agent that looks up order status and issues refunds gives a customer an incorrect refund amount. The team needs to determine whether the error occurred in the FM's reasoning, a specific tool/action group call, or the underlying data. What is the most effective debugging approach?

choices.text: Re-run the same prompt several times and use the most frequent refund amount as the correct value
Inspect the agent trace for each step, tool parameter, and tool result to find where it went wrong
Disable the refund tool until the issue is understood and process refunds manually meanwhile
Retrain the foundation model on correct refund examples so the error does not recur

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The agent trace shows each reasoning step, the tool called, its parameters, and the returned data, so the team can see whether the error came from the model's reasoning, bad parameters, or the tool's result.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Majority vote of reruns: doesn't find the cause.
• Disabling the tool: a mitigation, not a diagnosis.
• Retraining: premature without knowing the cause.

Key takeaway: diagnose agents step by step with traces.

stem: A team building a traditional tabular credit-risk model needs to explain individual feature contributions to each prediction, while a separate team building a Bedrock multi-step agent needs to explain its tool-use reasoning. Which pairing of tools is correctly matched to each need?

choices.text: Bedrock Agents trace for both the tabular model and the agent
Clarify SHAP for the tabular model; agent trace for the agent
Amazon Comprehend explanations for both use cases
SageMaker Clarify SHAP values for both use cases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify SHAP values explain feature contributions for traditional ML models such as tabular credit risk. Bedrock agent traces explain an agent's orchestration steps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Agent trace for both: can't attribute tabular features.
• Comprehend explanations: not an explainability tool.
• SHAP for both: doesn't show agent reasoning steps.

Key takeaway: match the explainability tool to the model type.

stem: Before any model is trained, a team must check whether one age group is under-represented in a lending dataset and whether approval labels are distributed differently between age groups. Which analysis fits this stage?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify post-training bias metrics computed on model predictions
SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift monitoring on the production endpoint
SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics such as class imbalance (CI) and DPL
SageMaker Data Wrangler quick model feature importance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pre-training bias metrics run on the dataset alone. Class imbalance measures under-representation of a facet (here, an age group), and DPL compares how often positive labels occur across facets. No trained model is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Post-training metrics: require a trained model's predictions, which don't exist yet.
• Model Monitor bias drift: monitors a deployed endpoint over time, which is later in the lifecycle.
• Quick model feature importance: shows which features drive a simple model, not whether groups are imbalanced or labeled differently.

Key takeaway: data-only fairness checks → pre-training metrics; prediction fairness → post-training metrics; production → bias drift monitoring.

stem: Before fully replacing a production customer-service FM with a newly fine-tuned version, a team wants empirical evidence that the new model performs at least as fairly and effectively across different customer segments before a full rollout. What approach best supports this?

choices.text: Test the new model in a lab environment with a curated set of representative examples chosen by the team
Skip evaluation, since the new model was fine-tuned on more recent data and should perform at least as well
A/B test a controlled share of live traffic and compare quality and fairness by segment
Replace the model for all traffic and monitor complaint rates by segment to detect regressions quickly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A/B testing a controlled share of live traffic compares quality and fairness by segment on real users while limiting risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Curated lab examples: may not reflect real traffic or segments.
• Skipping evaluation: assumes improvement.
• Full replacement then complaints: harm happens before detection.

Key takeaway: validate new models on real traffic with limited exposure.

stem: A team needs to evaluate whether a customer-facing FM's generated responses show inconsistent tone or helpfulness across different customer name/demographic cues embedded in otherwise-identical prompts, across tens of thousands of generated samples. Manual human review of all samples is not feasible. What approach is most appropriate at this scale?

choices.text: Use an LLM-as-a-judge to score responses against fairness criteria, with periodic human spot-checks
Skip fairness evaluation until the team can afford enough reviewers to read every response manually
Use aggregate Amazon Comprehend sentiment scores per customer group as the complete fairness assessment
Assign one engineer to read all tens of thousands of samples to ensure consistent judgment across groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An LLM judge applies consistent fairness criteria at scale, and periodic human spot-checks validate that the judge itself isn't biased.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Waiting for reviewers: delays evaluation indefinitely.
• Aggregate sentiment: too coarse for tone and helpfulness differences.
• One engineer reading everything: infeasible and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: scale with LLM judges; calibrate with humans.

stem: SageMaker Clarify post-training bias analysis reveals that a fine-tuned model's approval recommendations show a significant disparate impact against one demographic group compared to others, holding qualifications constant. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.text: Treat the finding as advisory, since Clarify metrics describe correlations rather than actionable problems
Increase the Bedrock guardrail hate speech filter strength on the model's recommendations
Deploy to production and use customer complaint rates as the primary fairness signal going forward
Investigate and fix root causes in training data and fine-tuning, then re-evaluate with Clarify

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A significant disparate impact must be investigated at its source (data representation, labels, fine-tuning), fixed, and re-evaluated with Clarify before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Advisory only: ignores a material fairness risk.
• Hate speech filter: unrelated to decision bias.
• Deploy and watch complaints: harm occurs first.

Key takeaway: fix bias at the source, then re-measure.

stem: A team is deciding whether to fully replace human fairness reviewers with an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline for evaluating generated content at scale. What is the key risk of full replacement that argues for retaining some human-in-the-loop review?

choices.text: LLM-as-a-judge cannot use Amazon Bedrock models as the judge, so a self-hosted model would be required
Human review is legally required for every generated output under AWS service terms
The judge model can carry its own biases, so periodic human validation of its scores is needed
LLM-as-a-judge is slower than human review per item, so it offers no benefit at scale

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The judge is itself a model that can carry systematic biases. Without periodic human validation, those biases can mis-score certain content consistently and go unnoticed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't use Bedrock models as judges: they can.
• Human review legally required for everything: not an AWS requirement.
• Slower than humans: it's much faster at scale.

Key takeaway: keep humans in the loop to audit automated judges.

stem: A company's responsible-AI policy prohibits its generative AI products from generating content that promotes competitors' products by name or gives medical diagnoses. Which Bedrock Guardrails configuration most directly operationalizes this policy at runtime?

choices.text: Denied topics for competitor promotion and medical diagnosis, attached to all relevant invocations
A SageMaker Model Card that documents the policy for each generative AI product in scope
A lower maximum token limit so responses are too short to include restricted content
Code comments referencing the policy document in each application's prompt module

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Denied topics encode prohibited subjects (competitor promotion, medical diagnosis) into a guardrail that's enforced on every invocation where it's attached.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model Card: documents but doesn't enforce.
• Lower max tokens: short responses can still contain restricted content.
• Code comments: not enforcement.

Key takeaway: policies must be enforced at runtime, not just written down.

stem: An external auditor wants evidence that a company's generative AI product both (a) is documented with its intended use, limitations, and risk assessment, and (b) technically enforces the organization's content policy at runtime. Which combination of artifacts should the team present?

choices.text: The Model Card plus the attached Guardrails configuration and CloudTrail logs showing it is invoked
Only the Guardrails configuration, since runtime enforcement also demonstrates that intended use was documented
Only the SageMaker Model Card, since documenting controls satisfies both the documentation and enforcement requirements
The company's general privacy policy, which describes how all AI products handle customer data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Model Card shows documented intended use, limits, and risks. The guardrail configuration plus CloudTrail evidence that it's used on invocations shows runtime enforcement. Together they cover both requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guardrails only: no documentation of intended use.
• Model Card only: documentation doesn't prove enforcement.
• General privacy policy: not product-specific evidence.

Key takeaway: auditors need both documentation and proof of enforcement.

stem: The legal team issues an urgent policy update requiring all customer-facing generative AI applications company-wide to immediately stop discussing a newly restricted topic. The company has 15 separate applications, each currently referencing its own independently configured Bedrock Guardrail. What is the most efficient way to roll out this change reliably across all 15 applications?

choices.text: Disable all 15 applications until each team confirms its guardrail has been updated
Have one engineer log in to each application's console and edit each guardrail individually
Push the same denied-topic update to all guardrails centrally, for example with infrastructure as code
Email each application team and let them update their own guardrail when convenient

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managing guardrails centrally, for example with infrastructure as code, lets one reviewed change roll out consistently and quickly to all 15 applications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling all apps: unnecessary outage.
• Manual edits by one engineer: slow and error-prone.
• Email to teams: inconsistent timing.

Key takeaway: policy changes at scale → centralized, automated configuration.

stem: A new engineer asks why the team maintains both Bedrock Guardrails and SageMaker Model Cards when both seem related to 'responsible AI.' Which statement best explains the distinct role each plays?

choices.text: Guardrails document policies for auditors
Guardrails enforce policy at runtime; Model Cards document intended use and evaluations
Guardrails and Model Cards perform the same function, so either one alone is sufficient for governance
Model Cards also block harmful content in real time, so Guardrails add only redundant protection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Guardrails actively enforce policies on each request. Model Cards passively document intended use, limits, and evaluations. They serve different governance needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Guardrails document for auditors: that's the Model Card's role.
• Same function: they differ.
• Model Cards block content: they don't.

Key takeaway: enforcement vs. documentation.

stem: A company runs a multi-tenant GenAI SaaS platform on Amazon Bedrock and needs to attribute token usage and cost to individual customer accounts for chargeback billing. Which approach provides the most accurate token-level attribution with the least custom infrastructure?

choices.text: Enable invocation logging with per-request metadata tags and aggregate token counts by tag
Use CloudTrail management events for InvokeModel, which include per-request token consumption for each caller
Query Bedrock model evaluation job reports, which include cumulative token usage broken down by tenant
Apply cost allocation tags to the Bedrock service so Cost Explorer reports token counts per customer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model invocation logging records token counts per request, and requests can carry tenant metadata, so logs can be aggregated per customer for chargeback. (Application inference profiles with tags are another option for cost attribution.)

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail management events: don't include token counts.
• Evaluation job reports: offline tests, not production usage.
• Service-level cost tags: can't split one shared service by tenant.

Key takeaway: per-tenant chargeback needs per-request usage data.

stem: A RAG chatbot passes retrieved passages plus the last 10 turns of conversation history into a 128K-context model on every request. Latency and cost have grown as conversations lengthen. Which change most directly reduces token consumption without materially harming answer quality?

choices.text: Summarize older turns into a rolling summary and keep only the last few turns verbatim
Increase the number of retrieved passages so grounding improves regardless of conversation length
Skip retrieval after the first user message and rely on the conversation history for later turns
Switch to a model with an even larger context window so history growth no longer causes errors

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Summarizing older turns into a rolling summary while keeping recent turns verbatim keeps essential context but shrinks tokens, lowering latency and cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More retrieved passages: adds tokens.
• Skipping retrieval after the first message: loses grounding.
• Bigger context window: postpones the problem at higher cost.

Key takeaway: compress conversation history; don't just enlarge the window.

stem: An engineering team notices that a document-summarization pipeline sends the same lengthy system prompt (containing formatting instructions and few-shot examples) with every request, consuming a large share of input tokens and cost. The team wants to cut input-token cost without changing the underlying model or degrading output consistency. Which two actions should they take? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase the temperature parameter so generated summaries are shorter and cheaper
Add more few-shot examples to the prompt so output needs fewer corrective retries
Switch the requests to streaming mode
Distill the static instructions into a shorter prompt or a fine-tuned model
Enable Bedrock prompt caching for the static prompt prefix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt caching reduces cost and latency for a repeated static prefix, and shortening the instructions (or moving them into a fine-tuned model) cuts recurring tokens directly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher temperature: doesn't shorten billed input.
• More few-shot examples: adds tokens.
• Streaming: changes delivery, not token cost.

Key takeaway: repeated static prompts → caching and compression.

stem: A product team is choosing a foundation model tier for a customer support triage feature that classifies incoming tickets into one of eight categories and drafts a short reply. Which model-selection strategy best balances cost and capability within a tiered-usage framework?

choices.text: Use the smallest model for both steps to minimize cost, and ask agents to edit weak drafts
Use a smaller model for classification and a larger model only for complex reply drafting
Alternate between a small and large model on each request to average out cost and quality
Use the largest model for every step to guarantee top accuracy on classification and drafting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Classification into eight fixed categories is a bounded task that a small model handles well. A larger model is only needed for nuanced reply drafting, so tiering keeps cost low without hurting quality where it matters.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Smallest model for everything: weak drafts push work onto agents.
• Alternating models: arbitrary and inconsistent quality.
• Largest model everywhere: overspends on the easy step.

Key takeaway: use the smallest model that meets each step's quality bar.

stem: A team evaluates two models for a summarization workload: Model A costs $0.003/1K input tokens and $0.015/1K output tokens with 92% human-rated quality; Model B costs $0.0008/1K input tokens and $0.0016/1K output tokens with 85% human-rated quality. Requests use 2,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens at 5 million requests/month, and the acceptable quality threshold for this use case is 80%. What is the most defensible cost-optimization decision?

choices.text: Alternate between both models evenly across all requests
Select Model B, which clears the quality bar far more cheaply, and escalate failures to Model A
Select Model A for all requests, because higher quality is worth the extra cost whenever customers read the summaries
Select whichever model has the lower per-token output price, since output tokens dominate summarization cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both models clear the quality threshold, so the cheaper model should take the bulk of traffic, and only low-confidence or flagged outputs escalate to the costlier model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Even alternation: pays for the expensive model on half the traffic for no reason.
• Always Model A: extra quality beyond the bar isn't worth the cost here.
• Lowest output price only: ignores input cost and quality.

Key takeaway: once quality is sufficient, optimize for cost with escalation.

stem: A media company needs to generate alt-text descriptions for 2 million product images by the end of the week, but the workload is not latency-sensitive and can tolerate results arriving asynchronously within 24 hours. Which approach minimizes cost while meeting the requirement?

choices.text: Buy Provisioned Throughput sized for peak and send all 2 million requests through synchronous InvokeModel calls
Submit a Bedrock batch inference job, which is asynchronous and cheaper per token
Send all 2 million requests concurrently through on-demand InvokeModel so the job finishes as fast as possible
Spread the workload across Regions with cross-Region inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock batch inference processes large, asynchronous jobs from S3 at a lower price than on-demand calls, which fits 2 million non-urgent requests with a weekly deadline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Throughput: priced for sustained real-time use and requires a commitment.
• 2 million concurrent on-demand calls: throttling and full on-demand price.
• Cross-Region inference: adds capacity, not a discount.

Key takeaway: large, non-urgent jobs → batch inference.

stem: A production application invoking a custom fine-tuned model on Amazon Bedrock experiences frequent ThrottlingException errors during business hours, even though on-demand throughput quotas were recently increased. Requests are consistent and predictable in volume from 9 AM to 6 PM daily. What is the most effective fix?

choices.text: Move the invocation code to AWS Lambda, which has separate throughput limits from Bedrock's own API
Buy Provisioned Throughput sized for the predictable business-hours peak
Keep requesting on-demand quota increases for the custom model until the throttling stops
Add exponential backoff retries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Custom (fine-tuned) models on Bedrock are generally served with Provisioned Throughput. Sizing it for the predictable business-hours peak removes capacity-driven throttling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda limits: the throttling comes from model capacity, not the caller.
• Repeated quota requests: don't guarantee capacity.
• Backoff only: smooths errors but doesn't add capacity.

Key takeaway: predictable demand for a custom model → Provisioned Throughput.

stem: A team is deciding between Amazon Bedrock prompt caching and a custom semantic cache built on a vector store for a document Q&A application where every request reuses the same 6,000-token system prompt and document context, but the user's question changes each time. Which statement correctly compares the two approaches for this scenario?

choices.text: A semantic cache is better, because it can cache complete responses regardless of prompt structure or wording
Prompt caching cuts cost for the repeated static prefix; a semantic cache keyed on varying questions rarely hits
Prompt caching works only through edge locations and cannot be used with direct API model invocation
Prompt caching and semantic caching solve the same problem, so either choice gives the same savings here

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Every request shares a large static prefix but asks a different question. Prompt caching discounts the repeated prefix, while a semantic cache keyed on whole questions would rarely hit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Semantic cache is better: few repeated questions means few hits.
• Edge-only prompt caching: incorrect; it works with direct API calls.
• Same problem: they optimize different things.

Key takeaway: repeated prefix → prompt caching; repeated questions → semantic cache.

stem: A retailer generates 2 million product descriptions with an LLM. Only about 1% change per day, when products are updated. The descriptions are shown to a global audience, and the goal is low latency worldwide and no model cost per page view. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: Purchase Provisioned Throughput so each page view gets a fast model response
Store outputs and serve via CloudFront; change keys on update
Put a semantic cache in ElastiCache in one Region that matches similar product requests
Enable Bedrock prompt caching so repeated page views reuse the cached prompt prefix

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The descriptions are effectively static content. Generate each one once, store it, and serve it from edge locations with CloudFront. Page views then cost no model calls and get edge latency. Versioned keys (or targeted invalidations) handle the 1% that change each day.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt caching: still invokes the model on every view. It only discounts the repeated prefix.
• Single-Region semantic cache: adds remote latency for global users and approximate matching for content that is exactly known.
• Provisioned Throughput: pays for capacity to regenerate content that doesn't need regenerating.

Key takeaway: if model output is reusable as-is, treat it as content. Cache the result, not the prompt.

stem: A support assistant returns answers of about 800 tokens that take about 12 seconds to complete, and users abandon the page before seeing anything. The team may not change the model, answer length, or capacity. Which metric should the fix improve, and how?

choices.text: Time to first token, by streaming responses (ConverseStream)
Throughput: buy Provisioned Throughput so the model generates tokens faster
Total generation time: reduce maxTokens so every answer finishes sooner
Tokens per second: raise the temperature so the model samples faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The problem is perceived latency. Users see nothing until the full answer completes. Streaming delivers the first tokens within about a second, and the rest continues to render, so time to first token and perceived responsiveness improve without changing the model, length, or capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lower maxTokens: truncates answers, which changes answer length and was not allowed.
• Provisioned Throughput: a capacity change, which is not allowed, and it doesn't necessarily reduce time to first token.
• Higher temperature: affects randomness, not generation speed.

Key takeaway: for long generations, stream. Users judge speed by time to first token, not total time.

stem: A voice assistant requires sub-500ms time-to-first-token for a natural conversational experience, but the current general-purpose foundation model averages 900ms time-to-first-token under normal load. The use case tolerates a modest reduction in reasoning depth. What is the best combination of actions to meet the latency target?

choices.text: Switch to Provisioned Throughput for the current model, which guarantees lower time to first token
Use a latency-optimized or smaller model, and cache responses for the most frequent intents
Add more few-shot examples to improve answer quality, accepting the added time to first token
Increase max_tokens so the model can plan its answer before streaming the first words

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Time to first token depends mainly on the model. A latency-optimized or smaller model shortens it, and pre-computed responses for the most frequent intents answer instantly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Provisioned Throughput: guarantees capacity, not lower TTFT.
• More few-shot examples: more input tokens, so slower.
• Higher max_tokens: doesn't speed the first token.

Key takeaway: TTFT targets → faster models and caching common answers.

stem: A RAG application backed by an Amazon OpenSearch Service vector index has grown to hold 40 million document chunks. Query latency for k-NN retrieval has degraded significantly, and recall has also dropped for some queries. Which combination of actions is most likely to restore both retrieval latency and accuracy?

choices.text: Store embeddings as plain text fields and compute cosine similarity in the application layer
Drop vector search and rely on keyword search, which scales better at 40 million chunks
Re-tune HNSW parameters (ef_search, m) and add shards or capacity for the larger corpus
Increase top-k per query so relevant chunks are still found despite the growing index

explanation:
Why this is correct:
As an HNSW index grows, its parameters (ef_search, m) and shard or compute capacity need retuning to keep latency and recall. Scaling resources to the corpus size addresses the degradation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Similarity in the application: doesn't scale to 40 million vectors.
• Keyword-only search: loses semantic recall.
• Higher top-k: more work per query, so slower.

Key takeaway: vector indexes need tuning and capacity as they grow.

stem: A legal-document search assistant using RAG must retrieve results for queries that include exact statute numbers, precise legal terms, and semantically similar concepts expressed in different wording. Purely semantic (dense vector) retrieval has been missing exact statute-number matches. What is the best retrieval strategy?

choices.text: Increase the embedding chunk size
Use hybrid search combining vector similarity with BM25 keyword matching
Keep vector-only search but lower the similarity threshold so more near matches are returned
Replace vector search with BM25 keyword search, since exact statute numbers are what matter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hybrid search combines BM25 keyword matching, which catches exact statute numbers and terms, with vector similarity, which catches related concepts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bigger chunks: don't fix exact-term matching.
• Lower similarity threshold: returns more noise.
• Keyword-only: loses semantic matches.

Key takeaway: exact terms plus meaning → hybrid search.

stem: A data science team needs to score 500,000 customer reviews for sentiment using a foundation model, with results needed by tomorrow morning but no requirement for individual real-time responses. Which throughput optimization approach is most appropriate, and why?

choices.text: Issue synchronous InvokeModel calls in a loop from one Lambda function to keep the implementation simple
Use Bedrock batch inference, built for large offline workloads at lower cost
Use response streaming for each request so the whole job completes in less total time
Raise on-demand quotas and send all requests concurrently to finish as quickly as possible

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Batch inference handles 500,000 offline requests from S3 at lower cost and without managing concurrency and retries yourself.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Synchronous loop in one Lambda: slow and hits the 15-minute limit.
• Streaming: helps perceived latency, not total job time or cost.
• Max concurrency with quota increases: throttling risk and full price.

Key takeaway: overnight bulk scoring → batch inference.

stem: An application generating long-form reports observes that overall throughput (reports per minute) is far below expectations even though the model's Provisioned Throughput capacity appears sufficient on paper. Investigation shows most requests specify max_tokens far higher than the actual typical output length, and many responses include verbose boilerplate the team doesn't need. What is the most effective fix to improve effective throughput?

choices.text: Increase the Provisioned Throughput commitment, since more model units always raise reports per minute
Reduce the number of concurrent requests so each report receives more of the model's capacity
Right-size max_tokens and trim prompt boilerplate to cut output generation time
Increase the temperature, which makes token sampling faster for long outputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generation time grows with output tokens. Right-sizing max_tokens and removing boilerplate from prompts and outputs shortens each request, raising reports per minute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More model units: costly if requests are longer than needed.
• Fewer concurrent requests: lowers throughput.
• Higher temperature: doesn't make sampling faster.

Key takeaway: shorter useful outputs = more throughput.

stem: A code-generation assistant must give stable, near-identical output for the same prompt, and a marketing-copy generator should vary its phrasing on each run. Which configuration is MOST appropriate, and what caveat applies?

choices.text: Set top_k to 0 for both so sampling is disabled and every run is fully reproducible
The same default temperature for both, because sampling parameters barely affect variation
High temperature for both, and fix the random seed so code outputs repeat exactly
Low temperature/top_p for code, higher for copy; temp 0 isn't a guarantee

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Temperature and top_p control how much the model explores less likely tokens. Low values make output more focused and repeatable, which suits code. Higher values increase variety, which suits creative copy. Even at temperature 0, providers do not guarantee bit-identical output, so downstream checks should validate structure or behavior, not exact strings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• High temperature with a seed: high temperature works against stable code output, and seed support and determinism vary by model.
• Same default for both: sampling parameters are the main lever for variation.
• top_k = 0: its meaning differs by model (it may not disable sampling at all), and it would also remove the variety marketing wants.

Key takeaway: tune sampling per use case, and design tests for 'stable enough' rather than exact determinism.

stem: A team tuning a creative-writing model finds that a high temperature setting alone sometimes produces incoherent or nonsensical output because low-probability tokens are occasionally sampled. They still want creative diversity but need to prevent selection of extremely unlikely tokens. Which parameter adjustment best addresses this?

choices.text: Increase max_tokens so the model has room to recover after it samples an implausible token
Lower temperature to zero, which removes randomness and guarantees coherent output
Set top-p to 1.0 and top-k to the maximum
Pair the high temperature with a top-p or top-k limit

explanation:
Why this is correct:
top-p or top-k limits sampling to more probable tokens, so a high temperature can still add variety without picking the low-probability tokens that produce nonsense.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More max_tokens: more room for nonsense.
• Temperature 0: removes the creativity needed.
• top-p 1.0 and maximum top-k: removes the limits entirely.

Key takeaway: temperature sets variety; top-p/top-k cut the unlikely tail.

stem: A GenAI application built on Amazon SageMaker real-time inference endpoints serves a workload with a predictable daily traffic pattern: near-zero traffic overnight, a sharp ramp at 8 AM, sustained peak from 9 AM to 5 PM, and a decline after 6 PM. The team wants to minimize cost while still meeting a strict SLA during business hours. What is the best resource-allocation strategy?

choices.text: Run the minimum instance count and rely only on reactive scaling to handle the morning ramp
Have an on-call engineer resize the endpoint at fixed times every day before and after the peak
Run a fixed instance count sized for peak traffic all day to avoid any scaling delays
Target-tracking auto scaling plus scheduled actions that pre-warm before the 8 AM ramp

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking handles unexpected variation, and scheduled actions add capacity before the known 8 AM ramp, so the endpoint doesn't pay for peak capacity overnight or lag at the ramp.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reactive scaling alone: lags the steep ramp.
• Manual resizing: error-prone.
• Fixed peak capacity: wastes money overnight.

Key takeaway: known patterns → schedule ahead; unknown → track targets.

stem: A SageMaker real-time endpoint hosting a foundation model is configured with target-tracking auto scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance, but during sudden traffic spikes users experience elevated latency and some request failures for several minutes before additional instances become available and healthy. What change would most directly reduce this scaling-lag impact?

choices.text: Move the model to Bedrock Provisioned Throughput instead of tuning the endpoint's scaling
Increase the scale-in cooldown period, because scale-in activity delays new scale-out actions
Disable auto scaling and run one very large instance permanently to absorb every spike
Shorten scale-out cooldown, lower the target, and keep a warm baseline of instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A shorter scale-out cooldown and a lower target trigger scaling sooner, and a warm baseline absorbs spikes while new instances start.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Moving to Provisioned Throughput: sidesteps rather than fixes the SageMaker scaling issue.
• Longer scale-in cooldown: doesn't speed scale-out.
• One large permanent instance: costly and still a limit.

Key takeaway: faster scale-out plus headroom for spikes.

stem: A team is deciding between Amazon Bedrock on-demand throughput, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, and a self-managed SageMaker inference endpoint for a new GenAI feature with highly variable and still-unpredictable traffic in its first three months post-launch. Which option is most appropriate initially, and why?
