Key takeaway: private access + model restrictions → interface endpoint with a policy.

stem: A platform team must guarantee that every model invocation by application roles uses the company's approved guardrail, even if a developer forgets to pass it in code. How can this be enforced?

choices.text: Store the approved guardrail ID in Parameter Store and require developers to reference it in code
Enable model invocation logging and alert whenever a request is made without a guardrail
Attach the guardrail to the foundation model in the Bedrock console so it applies to all callers
An IAM condition on bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier requiring the approved guardrail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier IAM condition key lets policies deny invocations that don't include the approved guardrail, which prevents calls without it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store reference: relies on developers.
• Logging and alerting: detective, not preventive.
• Attach to the model: guardrails are applied per request, not attached to models.

Key takeaway: enforce guardrail use with IAM conditions.

stem: Auditors require full prompt and response logging for a Bedrock application, but prompts frequently contain customer email addresses and credit card numbers that must not be readable in the logs by most engineers. Which approach meets these requirements?

choices.text: Disable model invocation logging and rely on CloudTrail management events for the audit trail
Enable invocation logging to an S3 bucket with Block Public Access and default encryption
Invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs with a data protection policy that masks sensitive data
Log only the input and output token counts for each request instead of the prompt text

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs captures prompts and responses, and a log group data protection policy masks email addresses and card numbers, with unmasking limited to principals with logs:Unmask.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable logging and use CloudTrail: no payloads.
• S3 with encryption: stores the raw sensitive data.
• Token counts only: fails the audit requirement.

Key takeaway: full logs without exposing PII → masking data protection policies.

stem: A support assistant receives a mix of trivial questions and complex troubleshooting questions. Using the most capable model for everything is expensive, and the team does not want to build and maintain its own classifier to choose models. Which Bedrock feature addresses this?

choices.text: Batch inference for every request to receive discounted per-token pricing
Intelligent prompt routing between models in a family
Cross-Region inference so requests are served from cheaper Regions automatically
Provisioned Throughput on the most capable model to lower its per-token cost

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Intelligent prompt routing sends simpler requests to a smaller model and complex ones to a larger model in the same family, without custom routing code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch inference: asynchronous.
• Cross-Region inference: capacity, not cheaper models.
• Provisioned Throughput: a commitment, not per-request model choice.

Key takeaway: mixed difficulty without custom code → intelligent prompt routing.

stem: Finance asks the GenAI team for a daily dashboard of token usage and cost for each of five applications that share the same foundation model. Which approach provides this with the least effort?

choices.text: Use the CloudWatch InvocationLatency metric per application as a proxy for cost
Parse each service's application logs and estimate tokens from character counts
Per-application inference profiles with cost allocation tags, plus their token metrics
Create a separate AWS account per application and compare the monthly bills

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An application inference profile per application gives each its own invocation identity, so token metrics and tagged costs can be split per application.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency as a cost proxy: inaccurate.
• Character-based estimates: inaccurate.
• Account per application: heavy and only monthly.

Key takeaway: per-app cost attribution → application inference profiles.

stem: An internal IT help bot receives many questions that are phrased differently but mean the same thing, such as 'reset my VPN password' and 'how do I change my VPN password'. The team wants to reduce model calls and latency for these repeated intents. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Increase the model's temperature so repeated answers are generated faster
Bedrock prompt caching, because it reuses stored answers for similar prompts
A semantic cache keyed on question embeddings
An exact-match cache keyed by the normalized raw prompt string

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A semantic cache matches questions by meaning (embedding similarity), so paraphrased questions reuse stored answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher temperature: unrelated.
• Prompt caching: reuses processing of identical prefixes, not answers to paraphrases.
• Exact-match cache: misses paraphrases.

Key takeaway: paraphrased repeats → semantic cache.

stem: A voice assistant needs the lowest possible time to first token on a supported model. The team is willing to pay a higher price per token for this part of the workload only. Which option should it evaluate?

choices.text: Batch inference with a shorter job timeout for voice requests
Latency-optimized inference for supported models
A global cross-Region inference profile to reduce latency
Increasing maxTokens so the model streams larger chunks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Latency-optimized inference is offered for selected models and Regions to reduce latency at a different price, which fits a voice use case willing to pay more.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch: asynchronous.
• Global cross-Region: throughput and resilience, not lower latency.
• Higher maxTokens: doesn't reduce TTFT.

Key takeaway: lowest latency, higher price → latency-optimized inference.

stem: Before launch, a team wants to measure whether its RAG system retrieves relevant context and whether generated answers are faithful to that context, across 500 test questions, without building a custom evaluation harness. What should it use?

choices.text: BLEU scores computed by comparing each answer with its source documents
CloudWatch InvocationLatency metrics collected during a load test
A knowledge base evaluation job with an LLM as judge
A careful human review of 10 randomly selected answers by domain experts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A knowledge base evaluation job with an LLM judge scores retrieval (for example, context relevance) and generation (for example, faithfulness) across all 500 questions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• BLEU vs. sources: measures overlap, not faithfulness.
• Latency metrics: not quality.
• 10 human-reviewed answers: too small a sample.

Key takeaway: evaluate RAG retrieval and generation at scale.

stem: An agent has two action groups: 'getOrderStatus' and 'getShipmentStatus'. Traces show the agent often calls getOrderStatus when users ask where their package is. Both APIs work correctly when called. What is the MOST likely fix?

choices.text: Clarify each action's and parameter's description
Add a guardrail that blocks the word 'package' in user requests to avoid the confusion
Increase the agent's idle session timeout
Switch the agent to a larger embedding model so similar tool names are separated better

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Agents choose tools based on descriptions. Clear, distinct action and parameter descriptions (what each returns and when to use it) fix wrong selections, and traces confirm the reasoning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking 'package': breaks legitimate requests.
• Session timeout: unrelated.
• Embedding model: agents don't choose tools by embeddings here.

Key takeaway: tool confusion → improve descriptions.

stem: Prompt changes have caused quality regressions in production twice this quarter. The team wants each prompt change to be automatically scored against a fixed set of reference questions before it can be promoted. Which approach meets this goal?

choices.text: Ask the model to rate its own answers in production and log the scores for weekly review
Increase model temperature in staging so edge cases surface before each release
Deploy every change to all users and roll back when the complaint rate increases
A pipeline stage that evaluates a golden dataset and blocks low scores

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An evaluation stage in the delivery pipeline scores each prompt change against a golden dataset and blocks promotion when scores drop.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-rating in production: not a gate.
• Higher temperature in staging: adds noise.
• Deploy then roll back on complaints: too late.

Key takeaway: gate prompt changes with automated evaluation.

stem: A report-generation feature returns documents that end mid-sentence. The Converse API response shows stopReason 'max_tokens'. Input size is well within the model's context window. What should the team do?

choices.text: Add a stop sequence at the end of the prompt so the model knows where the report ends
Reduce the input prompt length
Raise maxTokens or generate the report in sections
Lower the temperature so the model writes more concisely and finishes sooner

explanation:
Why this is correct:
stopReason 'max_tokens' means the output hit the configured limit. Raising maxTokens (within the model's output cap) or generating in sections fixes the truncation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop sequence: ends output earlier, not later.
• Shorter input: input is not the constraint.
• Lower temperature: doesn't guarantee shorter output.

Key takeaway: read stopReason to diagnose truncation.
